title: The Right File, the Right Time: How Prioritization Turns Outbound Subrogation into Enterprise Strategy
summary: Discover how smarter outbound subrogation prioritization helps insurers improve recovery performance, maximize capacity, and drive enterprise strategy.
body_markdown:
**By: Erin Powers, Vice President, Subrogation Business Solutions**


For many carriers, outbound subrogation has long been treated as a necessary part of the claims process, but not always as a strategic one. Because recovery work often begins after a claim has been paid, it can be viewed as a back-end function rather than a broader opportunity to improve claims’ performance. That mindset is changing.


In a recent[study on the future of auto subrogation](https://www.cccis.com/news-and-insights/posts/the-future-of-auto-subrogation-a-study-benchmarking-the-people-process-and-technology-shifts-reshaping-claims-recovery) , 85% of respondents said their organization leaders see subrogation as a priority investment area. That number reflects a broader shift in the industry, where leaders are indicating that subrogation is becoming a more visible lever for improving recovery performance, operational consistency, and claims efficiency.


And as leaders invest more attention in subrogation, a new question emerges: what could the operation do with more capacity? If teams could spend less time sorting through lower-potential files or chasing work that may not lead to meaningful recovery, where could that time be redirected? Toward more complex claims? Stronger negotiations? Better use of vendor partners? More consistent recovery decisions?


That is where outbound subrogation becomes a strategic opportunity: helping carriers direct time, expertise, and resources toward the recovery work that matters most.


## More Files Do Not Always Mean More Value


Outbound subrogation teams are often asked to find recovery opportunities across a large and complex claims environment. But more files do not automatically mean more value, and the challenge goes beyond volume alone. Timing plays just as large a role. A file worked too early, before there's enough information to make it actionable, can waste just as much time as one with limited recovery potential in the first place. Entering an auto claim a bit later might not hurt the outcome; what matters is getting the right file to the right person at the right point in time. Property and workers' compensation claims often follow a different timeline altogether, so the cadence for routing them to the team needs to flex accordingly.


That is why prioritization matters, not just what to prioritize, but when. The goal is to help teams reduce time spent on false positives, incomplete referrals, premature files, or claims that may not warrant the same level of review yet. With a clearer way to identify and prioritize claims at the right stage, carriers can help their teams focus attention where it is most likely to make a meaningful difference.


This is where subrogation becomes a capacity conversation. If teams could spend less time sorting through noise, what else could they do with that time? They could focus on more complex files, strengthen recovery positions, improve negotiation strategy, or move higher-value opportunities forward faster.


## The Sweet Spot Is Knowing What to Keep, What to Route, and What to Reconsider


Many carriers use a mix of internal teams, TPAs, collections partners, and outsourcing vendors to manage outbound subrogation. That mix can make sense, especially when teams are balancing volume, complexity, and capacity. But it also raises an important strategic question: which work should each resource handle? Some files may be appropriate for a more standardized process. Others may require internal expertise, especially when liability, documentation, estimate details, or negotiation strategy are more complex. In other cases, a carrier’s partner may be the right fit based on their thresholds, operating model, or available capacity.


The opportunity is to find the sweet spot. When carriers can better understand recovery potential and file complexity, they can make more intentional decisions about what stays with internal teams, what gets routed to a partner, and what should be deprioritized or revisited later. The goal is to be a thoughtful steward of that investment, directing resources, whether internal or third party, to the files where they create the most value, while protecting specialist time and giving leaders more control over how recovery work is managed across the operation. It also creates room to fast-track claims that are ready to recover, so a handler with the expertise to manage complex files can focus that expertise where it's needed most.


## Better Prioritization Can Turn Subrogation into Enterprise Strategy


As subrogation becomes a higher priority for claims leaders, the conversation is expanding beyond individual files. Leaders need to understand how recovery work is being identified, how it is being prioritized, who is handling it, and where time and resources may be better invested.


But having a strategy is only the first step. An enterprise strategy also requires insight to know whether it is working. Leaders need a clear view of where they are headed and a reliable way to measure progress along the way: were the assumptions behind the strategy correct? Is performance improving where it was expected to? Without that visibility, it is difficult to know whether prioritization decisions are paying off or where adjustments are needed. The right insights turn a static strategy into an evolving one that can be measured, tested, and refined as the business and the claims environment change.


## Precision Over Volume


The instinct when facing recovery pressure is often to add more: more staff, more vendors, more hours dedicated to review. But the real opportunity is not adding more effort into the same process but focusing that effort more precisely. When carriers can identify the right files, route them to the right resource, and do it all at the right time, they get more value out of the capacity they already have — a meaningfully different starting point than simply asking already-stretched teams to do more.


Outbound subrogation has always required carriers to detect subrogatable claims, prioritize the ones worth pursuing, and route them appropriately. What is changing is the strategic weight leaders are putting behind getting that right. With 85% of subrogation leaders saying their organizations see subrogation as a priority investment area, the opportunity is clear: approached this way, outbound subrogation moves beyond a back-end recovery function and becomes a meaningful lever for capacity, consistency, and enterprise strategy.
